quiz: According to Drucker, who is an “executive”?
Anyone with at least five subordinates
Any knowledge worker responsible for a contribution that matters to the organization
Only members of the executive committee
Anyone paid above a certain salary
The criterion is not the number of subordinates but responsibility for a contribution that affects the organization's results.
Where does Drucker recommend starting to become effective?
Write a strategic plan
Find out where your time actually goes
Reorganize your team
Set ambitious goals
Effective executives start with their time, first by recording it, because our perception of how we use it is almost always wrong.
Why group your discretionary time into large blocks?
To have fewer meetings
Because thinking work requires continuous time
To make reporting easier
Because short slots are reserved for emergencies
Fifteen minutes here and twenty there don't add up: substantive work requires long uninterrupted stretches.
Which question turns the executive outward?
What is my budget?
How many people do I manage?
What contribution can I make?
What are my tasks?
Asking what contribution you can make shifts attention from effort to results, which lie outside.
What does “building on strengths” mean in hiring?
Look for people with no weaknesses
Look for a major strength in an important area and make weaknesses irrelevant
Hire only generalists
Create a tailor-made job for each person
Looking for the absence of flaws produces mediocrity; Drucker recommends looking for the major strength.
What are “posteriorities”?
Tasks to delegate
What you decide not to do, or not now
Late projects
Next year's goals
A list of priorities without a list of posteriorities is just a wish list.
How should a generic problem be handled, according to Drucker?
Case by case, as it comes
With a rule or principle, once and for all
By handing it to a consultant
By waiting for it to disappear
Treating a generic problem as a series of isolated cases produces contradictory decisions.
Why does Drucker recommend starting from opinions rather than facts?
Because facts are expensive
Because choosing relevant facts already assumes a hypothesis, which is better made explicit and tested
Because opinions are always right
To go faster
Making opinions explicit as hypotheses to test protects against looking for facts that confirm what you already think.
